newsitem.title: USA: CVS had $60 million profit in 4th quarter.
newsitem.headline: CVS had $60 million profit in 4th quarter.

text.p: CVS Corp., the Northeast drugstore chain that became a stand-alone company in October, said Wednesday that it made a $60 million profit in the fourth quarter.

CVS, the nation's fifth-largest pharmacy chain, which used to be part of Melville Corp., said its net income for the three months ended Dec. 31, which equalled 53 cents a share, compared with a loss of $610 million, or $5.85 a share, in the 1995 fourth quarter.

The Woonsocket, R.I.-based company said its 1995 fourth-quarter results included $532 million in losses from discontinued operations, a pre-tax restructuring charge of $165.6 million and other one-time charges of $11.5 million.

CVS said its net sales for the quarter expanded by 14 percent to $1.55 billion from $1.36 billion, with pharmacy sales representing 43 percent of the total. Sales at stores opened at least a year increased 11 percent, it added.
It said operating profit from continuing operations in the quarter increased 30 percent to $89.1 million from $68.5 million in 1995 -- excluding the restructuring and other one-time charges.
For the full year, CVS said it had net income of $75.4 million, or 57 cents a share, which compared with a loss of $657.1 million, or $6.41 a share, a year earlier.

Sales for the year grew by 14 percent to $5.53 billion from $4.87 billion, with pharmacy sales accounting for 44 percent of the total. Sales at stores opened at least a year grew by 11 percent, it said.
"1996, by all measures, was an outstanding year for CVS, continuing our record of growth and industry leading performance," CVS Chief Operating Officer Tom Ryan said in a statement.

Ryan said the company's profit and sales gains were driven by continued strength in both pharmacy and non-pharmacy businesses, an aggressive new store opening strategy and significant cost reduction efforts.
At the end of the year CVS had 1,408 stores in 15 states, mostly in the Northeast, up from 1,366 stores at the end of 1995.
Ryan said growth in pharmacy sales reflected the company's ability to expand its share of the managed care marketplace and its programme to purchase pharmacy files from independents.

He added that CVS's non-pharmacy business benefited from gains in sales of over-the-counter medications, beauty products, photofinishing and greeting cards, as well as solid gains in private label products.
CVS's stock lost 50 cents to $44.375 in early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
